koster1994wwwtalk.title: Important: Spiders, Robots and Web Wanderers (www-talk mailing list, archived)
koster1994wwwtalk.author: Martijn Koster
koster1994wwwtalk.quote: Robots are one of the few aspects of the web that cause operational problems and cause people grief. At the same time they do provide very useful services.
supports: message header reads 'Fri, 25 Feb 1994 13:18:03 --100'
first public mention of a proposed standard letting server maintainers say which parts robots may access

the archived page shows the From line (m.koster@nexor.co.uk) and the subject; the To line 'Multiple recipients of list <www-talk@www0.cern.ch>' survives only in koster2019's quotation of the same message

koster1994spec.title: A Standard for Robot Exclusion
koster1994spec.author: Martijn Koster
koster1994spec.quote: This document represents a consensus on 30 June 1994 on the robots mailing list (robots-request@nexor.co.uk), between the majority of robot authors and other people with an interest in robots. [...] It is not an official standard backed by a standards body, or owned by any commercial organisation. It is not enforced by anybody, and there no guarantee that all current and future robots will use it.
supports: 30 June 1994 consensus date
'It is not enforced by anybody' appears verbatim in the Status section
the format has exactly two fields: 'The record starts with one or more User-agent lines, followed by one or more Disallow lines'
'Unrecognised headers are ignored.' - so no rate field can be added and relied on
motivation: 'certain robots swamped servers with rapid-fire requests, or retrieved the same files repeatedly'

rfc9309.title: RFC 9309: Robots Exclusion Protocol
rfc9309.author: M. Koster; G. Illyes, H. Zeller, L. Sassman (Google LLC)
rfc9309.quote: These rules are not a form of access authorization.
supports: header block reads 'Category: Standards Track' and 'September 2022'
abstract: 'originally defined by Martijn Koster in 1994'
the grammar is rule = *WS ("allow" / "disallow") *WS ":" - Allow is the field added since 1994
the strings 'crawl-delay', 'crawl delay' and 'rate' do not occur anywhere in the RFC text (grep of rfc9309.txt, 607 lines, zero hits)
Section 2.4: 'Crawlers SHOULD NOT use the cached version for more than 24 hours, unless the robots.txt file is unreachable.'
Section 3: 'The Robots Exclusion Protocol is not a substitute for valid content security measures.'
Authors' Addresses: Koster is listed independently (Wymondham, Norfolk, m.koster@greenhills.co.uk); only Illyes, Zeller and Sassman are Google LLC

koster2019.title: Robots.txt is 25 years old
koster2019.author: Martijn Koster
koster2019.quote: Then in September 1993 my Web server mailed me a report indicating someone had been retrieving an unusually large number of documents from my Web server. Further investigation indicated that at three points in time the same sequence of documents was retrieved at an enourmeous rate, in the order of 1 document per second.
supports: Koster quotes this passage from 'an old web page' of his own while going back through the archives in 2019
the server was 'an scrounged Sun 4/330 UNIX sever, connected to the internet over a company leased line (ISDN perhaps?), running a Perl web server'
'Charlie Stross describes overloading my server with his Websnarf crawler. I found emails from him from 7 Mar 1994'
'Back then it used /RobotsNotWanted.txt' - the file was renamed before the June 1994 consensus
the announcement of the finished standard was posted to www-talk on 'Sun, 3 Jul 1994 18:58:37 +0200'

stross2009.title: How I got here in the end, part five: "things can only get better!"
stross2009.author: Charles Stross
stross2009.quote: I was testing my spider and, absent-mindedly, gave it a wired-in starting URL. What I didn't realize was that I'd picked a bloody stupid place to start my test traversals from; a website on spiders, run from a server owned by a very small company - over a 14.4K leased line. I guess I'd unintentionally invented the denial of service attack! Martin, the guy who ran the web server, got in touch, and was most displeased. First, he told me to stop hammering his system - advice with which I hastily complied.
supports: Stross wrote the spider while teaching himself Perl during a burn-out at SCO
'I think I may have written the first spider to obey the robots.txt protocol; I'm certainly the numpty who necessitated its invention.'
this is a 2009 recollection of 1994, not a contemporaneous record

unverified: That Koster's server ran over a 14.4K line. Stross recalls '14.4K leased line' in 2009; Koster's own 2019 account says 'a company leased line (ISDN perhaps?)' and is explicitly unsure. The number is not in the prose.
That Websnarf caused the September 1993 bursts. Koster's 1993 report names no crawler, and the only Stross emails he could find are dated 7 Mar 1994.

Stross's claim that he 'necessitated' robots.txt. Koster's first public proposal is 25 Feb 1994, ten days before the only Stross emails Koster could find, so the surviving record cannot make Websnarf the trigger; the prose gives the dates it has and makes no causal claim.
How many documents the September 1993 bursts fetched in total. Only the rate survives.

Whether Martijn Koster was physically in Nottingham in 1994. Nexor was his employer and the mail is from nexor.co.uk; no source opened states the office location, so the box-tag names the organisation, not a city.

When Websnarf actually hit Koster's server. Koster found emails from Stross dated 7 Mar 1994 and says 'I'm not sure if there were others'; Stross's 2009 account gives no date. The prose therefore dates the correspondence, not the incident.
